scope: Second-ten preparation evidence only. Descriptive food processing and labelled historical/draft reports are not prescriptions. No import or publication permission is granted.
limitations: No database writes or new uploads occurred in this content review.
An EMA fennel page returned HTTP 429 on repeated access; a search listing is not a read monograph. No numerical fennel regimen is used.
The previous 55-row database snapshot is not a confirmed live target. Existing photos and botanical proposals do not clear medicinal content.

sources.title: The Medicinal Plants of the Philippines (1901)
sources.limitation: Historical report only. No clinical efficacy, modern safety clearance or human dosage is inferred; each record retains its exact entry and printed page.

sources.title: NParks: Growing Five Leafy Vegetables
sources.limitation: Only the Chinese Mustard paragraph is used. Boiling, steaming and stir-frying in the preceding Kailan paragraph are not transferred to mustard.

sources.title: NParks: Growing Five Root Vegetables
sources.limitation: Only the Radish paragraph is used. The thorough-cooking warning for the later Tapioca paragraph is not misattributed to radish.

sources.title: GardeningSG: Radish
sources.limitation: Cultivated Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus; not all wild Raphanus populations or medicinal preparations.

sources.title: NParks: Portulaca oleracea
sources.limitation: Food use of leaves, young shoots and flower buds; its traditional medicinal list is not clinical validation.

sources.title: NParks: Theobroma cacao
sources.limitation: Food-processing overview, not a domestic fermentation safety protocol or therapeutic dose.

sources.title: FDA: The FASTER Act: Sesame Is the Ninth Major Food Allergen
sources.limitation: Used for sesame-allergen recognition, not Philippine labelling law or medicinal efficacy.

sources.title: NParks: Cocos nucifera
sources.limitation: Food ingredients and processing; coconut milk, water and oil are different materials. No disease-treatment claim is adopted.

sources.title: Draft European Union herbal monograph on Zea mays L., stigma, EMA/HMPC/509424/2023
sources.limitation: Six-page draft, dated 24 September 2025, specifies corn silk (stigma), not tassels, grain or stems; traditional use is not well-established clinical efficacy.

sources.title: EMA: Maydis stigma
sources.limitation: The observed page still says draft under discussion. A closed consultation is not a final adopted monograph.

sources.title: NParks: Saccharum officinarum
sources.limitation: Sugar processing and botanical description; commercially grown sugarcane can be a multi-species hybrid, so this is not specimen authentication.

sources.title: NParks: Piper nigrum
sources.limitation: Dried-fruit food seasoning. Traditional disease claims are not adopted as proven treatment.

records.preparationDescription: Culinary use, not treatment: mustard leaves are eaten in salads or cooked; seeds are used in curries and pickles. The source does not supply cooking times or medicinal quantities.
historicalExclusions: No mustard poultice recipe is supplied in this entry; do not borrow Cleome viscosa instructions.
records.identityNotes: Reconcile the queue's Brassica juncea with the reviewed modern nothogenus proposal ×Brassarda juncea before import.
records.safetyNotes: No validated medicinal regimen is established by these food-use sources.

records.preparationDescription: Culinary use, not treatment: the swollen taproot is peeled, cut into small pieces and cooked in soups or meat dishes. The leafy tops may be stir-fried as a vegetable.
historicalExclusions: Do not convert the book's antiscorbutic claim into a medicinal recipe.
records.identityNotes: Raphanus sativus is treated in the modern GardeningSG page as cultivated Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus; retain the subspecies distinction.
records.safetyNotes: Food preparation is not evidence that radish cures disease.

records.preparationPart: Leaves, young shoots and flower buds
records.preparationDescription: Culinary use, not treatment: leaves and young shoots are consumed as vegetables; flower buds are added to salads. The reviewed modern source supplies no medicinal preparation quantities.
historicalExclusions: Withhold leaf-juice eyewash and treatment of coughing blood.
records.identityNotes: Olasiman here means Portulaca oleracea, not the existing Peperomia pellucida record sometimes called Ulasimang Bato.
records.safetyNotes: The historical eye and bleeding claims must not become self-treatment instructions.

records.preparationDescription: Food-processing overview, not treatment: seeds undergo fermentation and drying, then roasting, crushing, grinding and pressing to make chocolate products or cocoa butter. The surrounding pulp is eaten or processed into desserts. This is not a validated home fermentation protocol.
historicalExclusions: Withhold the book's stomach-dilation and theobromine diuretic claims.
records.identityNotes: Queue identity retained; modern Philippine occurrence and all-state duplicate checks still required.
records.safetyNotes: No therapeutic dose or condition-specific safety clearance is inferred from chocolate processing.

records.preparationPart: Leaves in the historical external report; seeds for allergen caution
records.preparationDescription: Historical description only: the book reports sesame-leaf poultices. This is not recommended as a home treatment; medicinal preparation instructions remain withheld.
historicalExclusions: Withhold emmenagogue baths and decoctions, purgative doses and castor-oil substitution.
records.identityNotes: No seed or leaf medicinal method is clinically cleared by the reviewed sources.
records.safetyNotes: Sesame is identified by the FDA as a major food allergen; avoid exposure when allergic. That guidance does not validate leaf treatment.

records.preparationDescription: Culinary use, not treatment: coconut flesh is shredded for desiccated coconut or squeezed to obtain coconut milk. Coconut milk is an ingredient in curries and desserts; oil is also extracted from the flesh. Coconut milk is not the liquid naturally inside the fruit.
records.identityNotes: Queue identity retained; no disease-specific preparation clearance inferred.
records.safetyNotes: The preparation describes distinct food ingredients, not a medicine.

records.preparationPart: Corn silk (stigma), not tassel, grain or stalk
records.preparationDescription: A draft EMA monograph describes cut corn silk as an oral herbal tea prepared by infusion or decoction. It addresses traditional use, not well-established clinical efficacy. No recipe or human dose is cleared here, and the book's tassel preparation is not substituted for corn silk.
historicalExclusions: Withhold the book's tassel and stalk diuretic recipes; tassels are not corn silk.
records.identityNotes: Modern evidence is plant-part-specific; the foliage photograph cannot confirm medicinal-grade stigma material.
records.safetyNotes: The draft does not recommend use below age 12 or during pregnancy/lactation, or when fluid intake must be restricted. Fever, painful urination or blood in urine require medical assessment.
publicationBlockers: Final monograph status and stigma-specific safety review

records.preparationDescription: Food-processing overview, not treatment: juice is extracted from the soft tissue of sugarcane stems and processed into sugar or syrup. No medicinal heating time, dose or cough treatment is supplied.
records.identityNotes: NParks notes that commercial sugarcane is often a complex hybrid; resolve the photographed specimen's species scope.
records.safetyNotes: Sugar processing does not establish medicinal benefit.

records.preparationPart: Fennel material in a shared historical fennel/coriander discussion
records.preparationDescription: Historical description only: the shared fennel and coriander passage mentions infusions and other extracts. It does not clear a modern, variety-specific preparation or human dose for this queue record.
historicalExclusions: Withhold the historical concentrated infusion and daily-volume regimen.
records.identityNotes: The species-level queue and photograph do not establish the sweet-fennel variety or medicinal fruit quality covered by a monograph.
records.safetyNotes: Do not transfer a sweet-fennel fruit regimen to unspecified fennel leaves, essential oil or another variety.
publicationBlockers: Full current fennel monograph and safety review

records.preparationDescription: Culinary use, not treatment: dried pepper fruits are used as food seasoning. NParks describes unripe fruits turning black when dried. No medicinal quantity or malaria regimen is supplied.
historicalExclusions: Withhold brandy-and-anise malaria treatment and purified-piperine dosing.
records.identityNotes: Piper nigrum is not Piper betle; do not transfer adjacent betel-leaf instructions.
records.safetyNotes: Food seasoning does not prove that concentrated pepper products or piperine treat disease.
